The Latest Report

Every phone starts as a hole in the ground. Lithium brine pools in the Atacama, where one iPhone’s journey begins: brine pumped from beneath a salt flat and left to evaporate for a year or more.

Latest Report · Friday, November 13, 2026

From Sand to Signal

One phone, five continents, and a single company that owns none of the factories: how an iPhone is made, from brine, rock and quartz sand to the retail counter, and who gets paid at every stop.

An iPhone is not made by Apple, and it is barely made in the place printed on the box. It is designed in California and Austin, its brain is fabricated in Taiwan by the only company on earth that can do it, its screen and camera eye come from Korea and Japan, its materials are converted to usable form overwhelmingly in China, and it is screwed together, at the end, by the cheapest and most replaceable labor in the chain, in China and now India. Assembly is the step everyone photographs. It is worth the least.

The money follows scarcity, not effort and not position. Apple, which owns no iPhone factory, files a gross margin of about 37 cents on every hardware dollar. TSMC, a contractor like Foxconn in form, files close to 60 cents, because there is no second TSMC. Foxconn, the largest private employer in the chain, files about 6 cents gross and 2 cents net, because Apple has spent twenty years making sure there is always a second Foxconn. The states understood this before the companies admitted it: China subsidized the assembly city, India now pays a cash incentive larger than the assembler’s entire profit on the phone, and the United States discovered in 2025 that a tariff gap between two country labels could move a quarter of world production faster than a decade of speeches.

So the phone in your hand is best read as a stack of chokepoints with an assembly hall at the bottom. The hall can move. It just did. The chokepoints, the refineries, the one fab, the two display makers, the one sensor maker, have not moved at all. That is the story of how it is made, and it is also the story of who gets paid.

From Sand to Signal · Evening Report

Four numbers, one argument

The chain is long. These are the numbers that say where its power sits.

90%Refined in China
China’s share of global rare-earth separation, and of graphite processing, for materials designed in California and dug up on four other continents.
$485Parts, box and assembly
TD Cowen’s bill-of-materials estimate for the 256GB iPhone 16 Pro Max, against a $1,199 price. The display and the rear camera are the joint-priciest parts, at $80 each.
6.25%The assembler’s gross margin
Hon Hai’s filed gross margin for 2024, on a consolidated basis. TSMC files 59.9%. Apple’s products margin is 36.8%. Scarcity, not chain position, sets the rent.
25%Now assembled in India
About a quarter of 2025’s iPhones, per Bloomberg, including every iPhone 17 model from launch day. Five years earlier the figure was close to zero. The United States assembles none.

THE BOARDPURPOSE

Why The Board exists.

I don’t have a ton of time. It’s hard to keep up.

There are so many conflicting narratives, fed by conflicting interests. It feels hard to know what is true, and I know I’m not alone in that.

I often have questions I want answered, or things I don’t understand, that the news simply doesn’t cover. Not all of the time, but sometimes. When that happens, there is nowhere obvious to go for a straight answer.

In my ideal world, I build something useful to me. Something I enjoy reading. Because if I do, so will other people, and it will help them too.

The Board is a personal project. Everything here reflects my own views and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or representative of my employer.
